tasks.title: Read three well rated registry modules and note what each one deliberately does not do.
Design a module by writing its variables and outputs before writing any resource.
Compose two of your own modules together rather than nesting one inside the other.
Tag a version of your module in git and reference that tag from a caller.
Declare a variable with an object type and use it to configure a resource.
Take a list of objects and create one resource per entry with for_each.
Use a dynamic block to generate repeated nested blocks such as security group rules.
Rewrite one dynamic block as plain repetition and decide which version you would rather maintain.
Rename several resources and use moved blocks so nothing is destroyed.
Move existing resources into a module and confirm the plan reports no changes.
Treat a no changes plan as the only proof a refactor was safe. Write that rule down.
Break it: refactor without moved blocks, read the destroy plan, then undo it before applying.
Write a review checklist covering hardcoded values, missing tags, open security groups and replacements.
Review your own configuration against that checklist and fix three findings.
Learn why a reviewer needs the plan output, not just the code diff.
Standardise naming across every resource using the locals pattern from day 133.
Generate module documentation automatically and commit the result.
Write a short document explaining what the configuration builds and why.
Link your day 117 recovery runbook to the code that would rebuild the environment.
Update your architecture diagram so it matches what the code actually creates.

days.title: Terraform In CI: Plan On Pull Request

tasks.title: Give the workflow AWS credentials using the least privilege approach from day 98.
Add fmt check and validate steps that fail the build on bad formatting or syntax.
Run terraform plan in the workflow on every pull request.
Post the plan output as a comment on the pull request so a reviewer can read it.
Confirm the pull request workflow never applies, only plans.

days.title: Terraform In CI: Apply On Merge

tasks.title: Add a workflow that applies on merge to main, targeting staging only.
Save the plan as an artifact and apply that exact plan rather than replanning.
Require manual approval before the production apply, reusing the pattern from day 96.
Confirm state locking prevents two workflow runs from applying at the same time.
Break it: push a change that fails validate and confirm nothing reaches AWS.
Install a static analysis tool for Terraform and run it against your configuration.
Read every finding and classify each as real, low priority or a false positive.
Fix the three most serious findings and rerun the scan.
Add the scanner to the pipeline so high severity findings fail the build.
Break it: open a security group to the whole internet and confirm the scanner catches it.
Read what policy as code means and how it differs from a static scan.
Write one rule that blocks any resource missing a required tag.
Wire the rule into the pipeline so a non compliant plan cannot be applied.
List five guardrails a real team would want enforced automatically.
Find a sensitive value inside your state file and understand why state must be protected.
Confirm no secret appears in your repository, your tfvars or your variable defaults.
Read a secret from AWS Secrets Manager with a data source instead of hardcoding it.
Write down what breaks when a secret rotates and how the configuration should handle it.
Break it: commit a fake secret, then practise the full response of rotating and cleaning up.
Collect three real Terraform errors and write what each one actually means.
Turn on debug logging with TF_LOG and read what the provider is really doing.
Use a targeted plan to isolate one resource, and read why targeting is a last resort.
Force replacement of a single resource and explain when you would want that.
Write a Terraform troubleshooting checklist and add it to your notes.
Read why an apply sometimes fails on a resource that was created moments earlier.
Configure timeouts on a slow resource and observe the difference.
Read the provider documentation for one resource end to end, including its import syntax.
Upgrade a provider version deliberately and read the plan for unexpected changes.
Read a provider changelog and find one breaking change from a past release.
Configure Terraform to assume a role into a second account or a separate environment.
Split your configuration so one apply cannot touch both staging and production.
Decide which resources belong in a shared configuration and which are per environment.
Read an output from another configuration using the remote state data source.
Write down the risk of one configuration depending on another one's state.
Install a cost estimation tool and run it against a plan.
Add the estimate to the pull request comment so cost is visible at review time.
Write a change that adds a NAT gateway and read what the estimate says.
Set a rule for what monthly increase requires a conversation before merging.

days.title: Bringing Hand Built Infrastructure Under Code

tasks.title: Pick a small set of resources you built by hand and list every one of them.
Write configuration for all of them before importing anything.
Import them one at a time until the plan reports no changes.
Resolve every mismatch the plan reports rather than ignoring it.
Write down how long it took and what you would do differently on a larger estate.
Create your ECR repository and its lifecycle policy in Terraform.
Define the CI deployment role and its policy in Terraform instead of the console.
Define the compute that runs your container, with the image tag as a variable.
Create the CloudWatch log group and retention setting in Terraform.
Apply and confirm your Month 4 pipeline still deploys successfully into it.
Decide whether infrastructure and application live in one repository or two, and justify it.
Define what happens when infrastructure and application both change in one release.
Pass the built image tag from the application pipeline into the infrastructure apply.
Run the whole thing: commit, build, push, apply, deploy, verify.
Document the full flow in a diagram from commit to running container.
Record the working state and the URL that proves the system is up.
Destroy the entire environment from code.
Rebuild it from code alone, with no console clicks, and time the whole process.
List every manual step you still needed and turn each one into a task to fix.
Fix the gaps, then destroy and rebuild once more to prove they are closed.
Have a friend break one thing in the Terraform layer without telling you what.
Diagnose it using plan output, state inspection and your day 156 checklist.
Fix it through code rather than by clicking in the console.
Have them change something in the console instead, then detect and reconcile the drift.
Write both incidents up with what broke, how you found it and how long each took.
Tidy the repository: README, module docs, diagram, and a clear getting started section.
Confirm every provider and module version is pinned.
Pin this repository on your GitHub profile alongside the Month 4 pipeline.
Read the Terraform Associate exam guide and map each objective to a day you have done.
List the exam objectives you have not covered and plan them into April.
Review your Terraform notes and mark what you still cannot write unaided.

questions.prompt: What is the sign of a well designed module?
options: It has a clear purpose with sensible inputs and outputs
questions.explanation: Modules that try to do everything become harder to use than writing the resources directly.

questions.prompt: Why design a module interface before writing its resources?
options: Because the interface is what callers depend on and is hardest to change later
questions.explanation: Changing inputs and outputs later breaks every caller, while internals can be rewritten freely.

questions.prompt: What does a dynamic block generate?
options: Repeated nested blocks inside one resource
questions.explanation: It is for repeated nested configuration such as a list of ingress rules.

questions.prompt: When should you avoid a dynamic block?
options: When plain repetition would be easier to read and maintain
questions.explanation: Clever configuration that nobody can read is a maintenance cost, not a win.

questions.prompt: What does a moved block let you do?
options: Rename or restructure code without destroying resources
Move a module to the registry
questions.explanation: It records the rename declaratively so Terraform does not see a delete and a create.

questions.prompt: What proves a refactor was safe?
questions.explanation: If nothing in the real world changes, the refactor touched only the code.

questions.prompt: Why does a reviewer need the plan output and not just the code diff?
options: Because the effect of a change is not always obvious from the code
questions.explanation: A small code change can produce a destructive plan, and only the plan shows that.

questions.prompt: What should an infrastructure code review checklist include?
options: Hardcoded values, missing tags, open security groups and forced replacements
questions.explanation: These are the categories where real damage and real cost come from.

questions.prompt: Why pin a module to a git tag rather than a branch?
options: So the code cannot change underneath you between runs
questions.explanation: A branch moves, and moving infrastructure code is how surprise changes happen.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of composing modules rather than deeply nesting them?
options: Simpler dependency chains and easier debugging
questions.explanation: Deep nesting hides what is actually being created and makes failures hard to trace.

questions.prompt: Why generate module documentation automatically?
options: So the documentation stays accurate as the variables change
questions.explanation: Hand written input tables go stale the first time someone adds a variable.

questions.prompt: What makes a naming convention worth enforcing?
options: Consistent names make cost tracking, searching and cleanup possible
questions.explanation: At scale, inconsistent naming is what makes an estate impossible to reason about.

questions.prompt: A refactor that produces a destroy and create plan is safe as long as it applies successfully.
questions.explanation: Recreating a resource can mean downtime or data loss, which is exactly what moved blocks avoid.

questions.prompt: An architecture diagram that no longer matches the code is worse than no diagram.
questions.explanation: People trust the diagram and make decisions from it, so a stale one actively misleads.

questions.prompt: Linking your recovery runbook to the code that rebuilds the environment makes recovery faster.
questions.explanation: The runbook stops being theory when it points at something that actually runs.

questions.prompt: What should a pull request workflow do with Terraform?
options: Run plan and show the output for review
questions.explanation: Plans on pull requests give reviewers the information they need before anything changes.

questions.prompt: Why apply a saved plan file rather than replanning at apply time?
options: So what was reviewed is exactly what gets applied
questions.explanation: Replanning can produce a different result than the one a human approved.

questions.prompt: Why should the pull request workflow never apply?
options: Because unreviewed code would reach real infrastructure
questions.explanation: The review gate only means something if nothing changes until after it passes.

questions.prompt: What stops two CI runs applying at the same time?
questions.explanation: The lock in the backend is what makes concurrent applies safe.

questions.prompt: What does a static analysis tool for Terraform look for?
options: Insecure configuration such as open security groups or unencrypted storage
questions.explanation: It reads your configuration and flags patterns known to be risky.

questions.prompt: How is policy as code different from a static scan?
options: Policies are rules you write and enforce, rather than a fixed set of checks
questions.explanation: Policy as code lets an organisation encode its own requirements, such as mandatory tags.

questions.prompt: Where do sensitive values end up even when you never write them in code?
questions.explanation: State records real attribute values, which is why the state backend must be protected.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to use a secret in Terraform?
options: A default value on a variable
Read it at runtime from a secrets manager
questions.explanation: The secret stays in the secret store and never lands in the repository.

questions.prompt: You committed a secret by mistake. What must you do?
options: Delete it in the next commit
Treat it as compromised and rotate it
questions.explanation: It is in the history and possibly already cloned, so rotation is the only real fix.

questions.prompt: Why fail the build on high severity scan findings?
options: So insecure configuration cannot reach production silently
questions.explanation: A warning nobody reads has no effect, while a failed build forces a decision.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible guardrail for a team to enforce automatically?
questions.explanation: Tagging affects cost allocation and cleanup, and humans forget it constantly.

questions.prompt: What should CI credentials for Terraform look like?
options: Scoped to what the deploy actually needs
questions.explanation: Least privilege applies to automation, and CI credentials are a high value target.

questions.prompt: Posting the plan output as a pull request comment makes infrastructure review practical.
questions.explanation: Reviewers can see the real effect without checking out the branch and running anything.

questions.prompt: Because state contains sensitive values, the state bucket needs encryption and restricted access.
questions.explanation: Anyone who can read state can often read secrets, so it must be treated as sensitive itself.

questions.prompt: A manual approval gate before production apply contradicts the goal of automation.
questions.explanation: Automating the work while keeping a human decision at the highest risk point is a normal pattern.

questions.prompt: What does TF_LOG give you?
options: Detailed logging of what Terraform and the provider are doing
questions.explanation: Debug logging is how you see the actual API calls behind a confusing error.

questions.prompt: Why is a targeted plan considered a last resort?
options: It applies part of your configuration and can leave things inconsistent
It does not work with modules
questions.explanation: Skipping the dependency graph is exactly how partial and surprising states happen.

questions.prompt: When would you deliberately force replacement of a resource?
options: When the resource is in a bad state that an update cannot fix
questions.explanation: Replacement is the blunt fix for a resource that has gone wrong in a way updates cannot resolve.

questions.prompt: Why does an apply sometimes fail on a resource created seconds earlier?
options: Cloud APIs are eventually consistent and the resource is not visible yet
questions.explanation: The create returned, but the rest of the platform has not caught up yet.

questions.prompt: What should you do before upgrading a provider version?
options: Run a plan and read it for unexpected changes
questions.explanation: Provider upgrades can change defaults, and the plan is where that shows up.

questions.prompt: Why split configurations so one apply cannot touch both staging and production?
options: To limit blast radius when something goes wrong
questions.explanation: A single mistake should not be able to take down both environments at once.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of reading another configuration's remote state?
options: It creates coupling, so a change in one can break the other
questions.explanation: Cross configuration dependencies are convenient until one team changes an output.

questions.prompt: Why show a cost estimate on the pull request?
options: So cost becomes part of the review rather than a surprise on the bill
questions.explanation: Reviewing cost at the moment of change is far more effective than discovering it later.

questions.prompt: What must you do before importing a hand built resource?
questions.explanation: Import populates state, so without configuration Terraform proposes destroying the resource.

questions.prompt: How do you know an import is complete and correct?
questions.explanation: A clean plan is the only proof that the code matches the imported reality.

questions.prompt: Why is importing a large estate slow?
options: Every resource needs accurate configuration written first
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is human work describing what already exists, not the tool.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of assuming a role across accounts in Terraform?
options: No long lived credentials, and clear separation between accounts
questions.explanation: Role assumption gives temporary access with an audit trail and no stored keys.

questions.prompt: Reading the provider documentation for a resource end to end is usually faster than guessing from examples.
questions.explanation: The arguments, behaviours and import syntax are all documented, and guessing wastes more time than reading.

questions.prompt: A change that adds a NAT gateway is a good example of something worth flagging at review time.
questions.explanation: It is a small code change with a recurring hourly cost, which is exactly what estimates catch.

questions.prompt: Fixing drift by clicking in the console is the correct long term response.
questions.explanation: Reconciling through code is what keeps the configuration authoritative, otherwise drift becomes permanent.

questions.prompt: Why define your CI deployment role in Terraform rather than the console?
options: So permissions are reviewable, versioned and reproducible
questions.explanation: Permissions are exactly the kind of thing that should go through review and live in code.

questions.prompt: Why pass the image tag into the infrastructure as a variable?
options: So the deployed version is explicit and traceable
questions.explanation: The infrastructure then records exactly which build is running.

questions.prompt: What is the argument for separating application and infrastructure repositories?
options: Different change rates, reviewers and blast radius
questions.explanation: Application code changes far more often than infrastructure, and the risk profiles differ.

questions.prompt: What does a successful destroy and rebuild prove?
options: That the environment is genuinely reproducible from code
questions.explanation: Any manual step you still need is a gap in the configuration, and this exercise finds them.

questions.prompt: You needed a manual step during the rebuild. What is the correct response?
options: Turn it into a task and close the gap in code
questions.explanation: Documented manual steps quietly become permanent, which defeats the purpose.

questions.prompt: How should you fix a fault that someone introduced in the Terraform layer?
options: Click the fix in the console
Fix it in code and apply
questions.explanation: Fixing outside the code creates drift and hides the real change from everyone else.

questions.prompt: Why pin every provider and module version before calling a project finished?
options: So the configuration still produces the same result months later
questions.explanation: Reproducibility over time is the point, and unpinned versions quietly break it.

questions.prompt: What makes an infrastructure repository useful to an employer?
options: Readable code, pinned versions, documentation and a working pipeline
questions.explanation: Reviewers look for judgement and maintainability, not volume.

questions.prompt: Why map exam objectives to days you have already completed?
options: To find the gaps precisely instead of revising everything evenly
questions.explanation: Targeted revision is the only efficient way to prepare when time is limited.

questions.prompt: What is the value of writing up both a code fault and a drift incident?
options: They are different failure modes and both come up in interviews
questions.explanation: One is a code problem and the other is a process problem, and explaining both shows real understanding.

questions.prompt: What should the getting started section of your README contain?
options: The exact commands to run the project from a clean machine
questions.explanation: Someone should be able to clone the repository and get it running without asking you.

questions.prompt: Which statement demonstrates the most capability?
options: Built a reviewed pipeline that plans on pull requests and applies on merge with approval gates
questions.explanation: Describing the working process shows how you operate, not just which tool you touched.

questions.prompt: Cost estimation in the pull request turns cost into a review decision rather than a monthly surprise.
questions.explanation: The point is to make the trade off visible at the moment somebody can still change it.

questions.prompt: Manual steps in a rebuild are acceptable as long as they are documented.
questions.explanation: Documented manual steps become permanent and are exactly what infrastructure as code exists to remove.

questions.prompt: Mapping the exam guide against your completed work is a better plan than starting revision from scratch.
questions.explanation: Most of the syllabus is already covered by what you built, and only the gaps need new study.
